question: For six weeks a customer-service lead has typed the same three corrections about tone and terminology into every new chat in her team's project. What should she do about that?
options: A) Keep the three corrections in a note she can copy, so retyping them into each new chat takes only a moment.
B) Move the three corrections into the project's standing instructions, so chats there start with them applied.
C) Add the three corrections at the end of each chat instead, so they are the most recent thing in the conversation.
D) Ask at the start of each chat whether the three usual corrections are understood before the real work begins.
correct_answers: B) Move the three corrections into the project's standing instructions, so chats there start with them applied.
explanations: A copyable note reduces the typing but keeps the requirement dependent on her remembering, and colleagues in the same project still do without it.

Correct. A correction needed in every chat is standing context rather than a per-chat instruction. Project instructions apply to every conversation in that project, which makes the fix durable and available to the whole team.
Moving corrections to the end of a chat applies them after the work has been produced, so each conversation still starts from the wrong footing.
A confirmation exchange at the start costs a turn and establishes nothing that survives into the next conversation.
